subtitle: Support employee resource groups through open participation, clear sponsorship, approved work time and realistic privacy expectations. Learn to invite useful contributions while respecting workload and formal reporting duties.
audience: For supervisors, managers, HR partners and ERG leaders or members at DHS and DSD. It explains how to support ERGs and where their limits are.

lessons.title: What ERGs and affinity spaces are in state service
objectives: Describe the purpose and three guiding principles of State of Minnesota enterprise employee resource groups.
Explain the open membership rule for enterprise ERGs and how it relates to affinity spaces.
Identify what ERGs are not for, including bargaining and grievances.
Distinguish an enterprise ERG from an informal team gathering or a formal consultation process.
lessons.teaching:
Employee resource groups, or ERGs, bring employees together around shared identities or experiences and welcome colleagues who support their purpose. Minnesota Management and Budget coordinates enterprise groups across state agencies. Their guiding principles are culture, career development and community building, with regular meetings for support and learning. The MMB directory identifies current groups and application arrangements; use that page rather than assuming a previously published list is complete or that applications are always open.

The enterprise rules allow participation by state employees who support the group's goals, including allies. Sharing the group's identity is not a condition of membership. Employees should not have to prove a personal identity to express interest, and supervisors should not infer identity from attendance. Membership, participation and leadership still have relevant rules about conduct, approvals and duties. Being welcome in a group does not remove those rules or ensure that every request for work time is approved.

An affinity space is a general term for a gathering focused on shared experience. That focus can help participants choose what to discuss, but it does not by itself authorize excluding employees from an enterprise ERG activity. Explain the purpose, ways to take part and discussion rules before the event, with access needs in mind. Ask MMB about event-design questions rather than inventing an identity test or treating a group label as permission to restrict entry. People can join the discussion without telling their own life story.

Keep the group's work within its role. Enterprise guidelines exclude bargaining over employment terms and handling grievances or labor disputes. Use the applicable union and labor relations routes for those matters. An ERG does not investigate discrimination complaints or replace Human Resources and Equal Opportunity and Access. If a concern arises during a meeting, members retain the reporting duties attached to their jobs. A supervisor cannot postpone a required report because the discussion occurred in a voluntary group.

Employee perspectives can inform agency questions, but they do not represent everyone who receives DHS services. Engage the people affected by a service proposal through the appropriate program process. Where Tribal implications arise, coordinate with the DHS Tribal liaison so authorized officials can follow the formal consultation process. ERG participation supports employee community and development; it does not confer authority to act for a Tribal government or decide a service policy.
lessons.keyPoint: Enterprise ERGs are open to all, including allies, and exist for culture, career development and community. They are not a bargaining table, a complaint channel or a substitute for formal consultation.
lessons.example: Practice case: Lucian, a DSD supervisor, learns that one of his staff, Marisol, attends an enterprise ERG for employees of a particular heritage. Another staff member, Bram, tells Lucian he would like to join the same ERG to learn and support colleagues, but assumes he is not allowed because he does not share that heritage. Lucian is not sure what the rules are.
lessons.question: What should Lucian tell Bram?
choices: That he should ask Marisol whether the group would accept him.
That enterprise ERG membership is open to all state employees, including allies, and he can check the MMB ERG page and talk with Lucian about fitting meetings into his schedule.
That ERGs are only for people who share the identity, so he should look for a different group.
feedback: Marisol may choose to discuss her experience, but she does not decide the enterprise membership rules. Lucian can use the public guidance without making her responsible for approving a colleague’s interest.
This is the best response. It reflects the enterprise guidelines, points Bram to the official source and keeps the supervisor's role focused on time and workload.
This is inaccurate for enterprise ERGs, which are open to all, including allies who support the group's mission.
lessons.reflection: What do you imagine happens in an ERG you have never attended? Where did that picture come from, and how might you check it?
lessons.action: Visit the MMB State of Minnesota ERGs page and read the enterprise guidelines. Note the three principles and the rule about what ERGs cannot be used for, and share the page link with your team.

check.question: Which activity do the enterprise ERG guidelines say ERGs may not be used for?
check.correct: Negotiating terms and conditions of employment or addressing grievances.
wrong: Offering career development events for members.
check.feedback: Career development and cross-agency connection are core ERG purposes. Bargaining over working conditions and grievances belongs to unions and labor relations, and the guidelines exclude them from ERG activity.

lessons.title: Sponsorship without extracting unpaid labor
objectives: Describe the roles of executive sponsor, champion and chair in an enterprise ERG.
Identify requests to ERG members that amount to unrecognized work.
Plan how to ask for ERG input in a way that is voluntary, scoped and credited.
Explain why ERG input does not replace formal consultation or engagement.
lessons.teaching:
An enterprise ERG has several leadership roles with different responsibilities. Under MMB's bylaws, an executive sponsor is an agency head or designee who provides guidance; a director-level champion supports the work, and members elect chairs or co-chairs. These roles connect the group with leaders and help organize its commitments. MMB's disability-retention guidance encourages regular leadership contact with employee groups as one way to learn about workplace concerns.

That connection can create demands on members' time. A policy review, event, recruitment discussion and panel presentation may each sound manageable while together competing with core assignments. Look at existing work and who keeps receiving requests instead of assuming that interest in a topic creates spare time. An employee may welcome a development opportunity, decline it or need a different schedule. Those choices do not show how much they care about colleagues or the community.

Before requesting input, ask the chair how the group receives proposals and explain the purpose, questions, deadline and expected effort. Invite a manageable contribution that members can decline without pressure from the requester. Agree on work time and coverage with supervisors before making promises. An invitation alone cannot approve pay, overtime or a change to assigned duties. Check the applicable ERG participation rules and refer uncertain pay questions to Human Resources. If the task is a continuing agency responsibility, discuss an approved assignment or properly resourced role instead of relying indefinitely on volunteer availability.

Discuss how the contribution will be used and credited before collecting it. Ask whether contributors want acknowledgment, while explaining that required records and disclosure rules still apply. Do not promise that choosing no public credit makes participation confidential. For a presentation, confirm who is speaking, in what capacity and what approvals are needed; an ERG leadership title does not itself authorize someone to speak for MMB or an agency.

Members offer their own views and may know a great deal about the issue. Their views still cannot stand for everyone who receives services. Use their input to identify questions and examine assumptions, then engage affected communities through the program's proper process. Equity analysis can organize evidence and engagement; it does not replace formal Tribal consultation, legal review or the authority of the person responsible for a decision.
lessons.keyPoint: Treat substantial requests to ERGs as work: scoped, voluntary, recognized in workload and credited. ERG input informs leaders but does not replace formal consultation.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD manager, Evander, is finalizing a new outreach plan for disability waiver services and has a tight deadline. He emails the co-chair of the enterprise ERG for employees with disabilities, Ottilie, asking her to gather members' feedback on the full plan within three days and to recruit two members to present at the county partner meeting. Ottilie is a program analyst with her own full workload in another agency.
lessons.question: What is a better way for Evander to approach this?
choices: Send the same request to several ERGs, so the work is spread more widely.
Keep the request as is, since ERG members care about these issues and will want to help.

Ask Ottilie how the group prefers to receive requests, narrow the ask to specific questions with realistic time, make participation clearly optional, offer to coordinate work time with supervisors and credit contributors, and use formal engagement for the plan itself.
feedback: Spreading the request does not change the core problem: unscoped, unrecognized work on a short deadline. It multiplies the burden.

Interest in the topic does not establish available capacity. The full-plan review and presentations require explicit scope, time and approval; do not assume members will absorb them alongside existing assignments.

This is the best response. Agree on scope and timing, make the invitation optional and confirm approved time before work begins. Credit choices do not override record requirements, and a service decision still needs appropriate engagement and authority.
lessons.reflection: Have you ever been asked to speak for a group you belong to, or asked someone else to? How was the time and effort recognized?
lessons.action: Before requesting ERG input, write the purpose, questions, time and deadline. State that the invitation is optional, how work-time approval will be arranged and how contributions will be used. Discuss credit and privacy limits before collecting responses.

check.question: Why should ERG feedback not be treated as the community engagement for a service decision?
check.correct: ERG members speak as employees from their own experience and are not a representative voice for the people DHS serves.
wrong: Because ERGs are not allowed to discuss anything related to DHS programs.
Because ERG feedback is always less accurate than data.
check.feedback: ERG members may have valuable insight, and ERGs can discuss work topics within their purpose. But their input is not a substitute for engaging the communities affected by a decision, and they should not be asked to represent those communities.

lessons.title: How supervisors support time and recognition
objectives: Explain the bylaws' provisions on paid work time, supervisor discretion and approval for leadership roles.
Apply supervisor discretion consistently across different ERGs and staff.
Plan workload coverage so an employee can take part in ERG activities.
Identify ways to recognize ERG leadership as professional development.
lessons.teaching:
When supporting an ERG request, consider both the group’s purpose and the employee’s assigned work. The enterprise bylaws permit paid time for qualifying meetings and events during a normal schedule, while supervisors retain discretion for workload and overtime. Leadership roles require supervisor approval. These rules support taking part, but they do not make every activity paid work. Essential services still need coverage while an employee is away.

MMB's join guidance explains that outside-hours participation is normally unpaid. For a non-exempt employee, an assigned work activity or attendance directly related to normal duties is an exception. The bylaws also exclude community service, charitable and social events from paid work time, with authorized leave an option during scheduled hours. Confirm uncertain event classifications, scheduling or pay questions with MMB and Human Resources before making a commitment. Do not promise that unpaid participation or informal evening make-up time resolves a pay issue.

Use the same criteria instead of valuing one group’s identity or topic more highly than another’s. Consider the activity, time needed, essential duties and coverage options. A public-facing role with no available coverage may require a different arrangement from a role with flexible deadlines. Explain the actual constraint and consider another date or participation method. A different result can be justified by different work needs; consistent review does not mean every request receives the same answer.

For recurring meetings, agree on schedules and handoffs before the employee is away. Coordinate calendar details without unnecessarily advertising a person's group membership or possible identity. If support remains unresolved after discussion, the MMB join page directs employees to their agency's Human Resources team for guidance. Do not promise that this step guarantees approval, and do not penalize someone for seeking appropriate guidance.

ERG leadership may provide practice in facilitation, planning and cross-agency work. Ask whether the employee wants to include those development experiences in a plan or conversation. Avoid treating voluntary participation as a measure of loyalty or personal commitment. At the same time, employees and supervisors must maintain necessary approval, timekeeping and work records. Ask for what you need to apply the rules, not a person’s identity or a list of all their groups. Development choices do not cancel formal evaluation or recordkeeping responsibilities.
lessons.keyPoint: Review ERG time requests consistently against the activity, schedule and coverage rules. Confirm leadership approval and pay questions, and distinguish optional development recognition from required work records.
lessons.example: Practice case: Two analysts on a DSD data team ask their supervisor, Cordelia, for time to attend enterprise ERG meetings. Fenna wants to attend a monthly meeting of an ERG for parents. Thaddeus has been elected co-chair of another ERG, which will take about four hours a month. The team has a large data submission due in six weeks. Cordelia wants to be fair to both and protect the deadline. Both requests involve qualifying business activities within normal hours, and Cordelia has confirmed that coverage can be arranged without overtime.
lessons.question: What should Cordelia do?
choices: Approve Fenna's monthly attendance, approve Thaddeus's leadership role, work with both on a coverage plan around the submission, and ask Thaddeus whether he would like the co-chair role reflected in his development plan.
Approve both but ask them to make up the time by working evenings.
Deny both requests until after the data submission, then revisit.
feedback: This is the best response under the stated conditions: qualifying activities, feasible coverage and no overtime. Confirm approval and the work plan, then offer optional development recognition without treating participation as proof of identity or commitment.

The bylaws allow paid work time for ERG activities within the normal schedule. Requiring make-up time treats ERG participation as a personal favor rather than an allowed activity and may raise pay questions for non-exempt staff.
A workload limit can be appropriate when coverage is unavailable. Here, Cordelia has confirmed a workable plan, so a blanket six-week denial does not address the actual circumstances.
lessons.reflection: If you supervise, how consistent is your approach to requests for time for ERGs, trainings and other development? What would an employee on your team say?
lessons.action: Review the MMB participation guidance with the relevant supervisor. Identify the activity, schedule, approval and coverage needed, and route uncertain pay questions to Human Resources before attendance.

check.question: Under the enterprise ERG bylaws, what must an employee get before serving as an ERG chair or co-chair?
wrong: A written statement confirming they share the group's identity.
check.feedback: Leadership roles require supervisor approval because of the time involved. No identity statement is required, since membership is open to all, including allies.

lessons.title: Confidentiality, data and boundaries
objectives: Explain why ERG participation can involve sensitive personal information.
Describe how the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act affects ERG communications on state systems.
Identify where to route harassment, discrimination or working-conditions concerns that come up in an ERG setting.
Draft a group agreement that sets realistic expectations about privacy.
lessons.teaching:
People may assume that ERG members share an identity, even though allies can also attend. Avoid guessing or sharing personal details without a valid reason. A supervisor may need basic event and scheduling information to approve time, but that does not justify asking for personal histories or a list of an employee's affiliations. Explain why information is needed and use the appropriate work record rather than discussing it casually with others.

An employee group cannot make government data confidential just by creating them. Minnesota Statutes section 13.03 starts with public access unless a statute, valid temporary classification or federal law provides otherwise. Different parts of a record may have different protections under those rules. Ask the responsible data-practices staff about classification, access and sharing; an organizer should not make a release decision from the group's name or the storage platform alone.

The enterprise bylaws require meeting records and make them subject to data-practices and retention requirements. Record decisions, actions and necessary business details while avoiding unnecessary personal stories in broadly shared minutes. Keep any required complaint or personnel record in its authorized channel. Do not erase existing notes, omit required facts or promise that no names will ever be recorded. Section 13.05 limits collection and use of information about individuals; responsible records staff can help determine what is needed and who may receive it.

A group agreement can ask members not to repeat personal stories or pressure anyone to disclose. It should also explain that the group cannot guarantee anonymity, legal confidentiality or compliance by every participant. Required reporting and authorized records duties continue. Even without a name, details about a role or event may reveal who a story concerns. Plan access to meeting notes and explain these limits before inviting sensitive discussion.

If someone describes possible protected-class harassment or discrimination, offer support and use the designated agency reporting process. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must report allegations immediately to Human Resources or the affirmative action officer; DHS requires prompt referral to Equal Opportunity and Access. Do not wait for the person's permission or conduct an ERG investigation before fulfilling that duty. Explain the referral and share only what the authorized process requires. EAP may provide personal support, and a union may advise a member, but neither contact substitutes for a required agency report. Use the relevant emergency or safety route for immediate danger, and refer bargaining or grievance matters through labor relations and the union.
lessons.keyPoint: Set realistic privacy expectations, keep necessary records in authorized channels and fulfill reporting duties promptly. Group norms cannot override data law, records requirements or formal complaint processes.
lessons.example: Practice case: At an enterprise ERG meeting held over the state video platform, a member from DHS, Anselm, describes repeated comments from a coworker about his faith and says he does not know what to do. The ERG secretary, Wilhelmina, is preparing the business minutes for the group’s shared channel but has not posted them. Any notes already created will be handled under the applicable records rules. A member who is also a supervisor at DHS, Rhiannon, was on the call.
lessons.question: What is the best way for the group to handle this?
choices: Post detailed notes so there is a record that can support a future complaint.

Keep Anselm's account out of the notes, have someone check in with him afterward and share routes including HR and EOAD, and have Rhiannon make sure the concern reaches HR or EOAD, telling Anselm she will do so.
Have the ERG draft a letter to Anselm's division director describing the problem.
feedback: Broadly posting the account could expose personal details and does not replace a formal report. Necessary records are not solely Anselm’s responsibility: the supervisor and authorized staff must meet their own reporting and recordkeeping duties.

This is the best response when “notes” means the broadly shared business minutes. Rhiannon must report promptly through the required route and explain that step; permission is not a prerequisite. Preserve necessary facts and existing records in authorized channels rather than deleting them or promising secrecy.
ERGs are not a complaint channel. A group letter bypasses HR and EOAD and exposes Anselm's situation to more people.
lessons.reflection: What would you want to know about privacy before sharing something personal in a group at work? How could your team or group make that clearer?
lessons.action: Propose a group agreement covering necessary business notes, limits on sharing personal stories, records retention and required reporting. Confirm uncertain classifications with data-practices staff before collecting or sharing sensitive information.

check.question: Under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, what is the starting presumption for data a government entity creates or maintains?
check.correct: The data are public unless a law classifies them otherwise.
wrong: The data are private unless the person consents to release.
The data are confidential if they relate to an employee group.
check.feedback: Minnesota Statutes section 13.03 presumes government data public unless classified by law. Some employee data are private, but a group label does not make data confidential. Plan ERG communications with that in mind.

cards.back: A cross-agency employee resource group coordinated by MMB, open to all state employees including allies, focused on culture, career development and community building.
A gathering focused on shared experience. The label does not itself authorize identity-based restrictions in an enterprise ERG; confirm event arrangements with MMB.
An agency head or designee who provides leadership and guidance to an ERG and connects it with decision-makers.
Requests for input, events or outreach whose time and effort have not been addressed in approved workload plans. Examine actual assignments rather than assuming anyone has spare capacity.

Government data are presumptively public under section 13.03, subject to applicable classifications. Ask data-practices staff about a particular record rather than assuming all ERG material has one status.

aid.heading: Supervisor checklist for ERG requests
items: Confirm the activity’s business purpose and applicable participation rules.
Review schedule, workload, coverage and overtime implications before approving time.
Apply consistent criteria while considering actual job requirements.
Consider coverage or another participation option when a constraint arises.
Confirm leadership approval and offer optional development recognition.
Request necessary approval information without probing identity or unrelated affiliations.

aid.heading: Before asking an ERG for help
items: Ask the chair how the group wants to receive requests.
State scope, time needed and deadline.
Confirm approved work time and coverage with supervisors before work starts.
Discuss credit preferences while explaining required records and privacy limits.
Arrange appropriate community engagement and formal Tribal consultation where needed; ERG input does not replace them.

aid.heading: Privacy and routing
items: Keep necessary business records and avoid unnecessary personal details in shared minutes; preserve existing records under retention rules.
Explain that group norms cannot guarantee anonymity or legal confidentiality.
Fulfill immediate supervisory reporting and DHS referral duties; support contacts do not replace required reports.
Use union and labor relations channels for bargaining and grievances.
Confirm classification, collection and disclosure questions with data-practices staff.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — State of Minnesota ERGs
sources.note: Current directory, group purposes and application information. The page currently notes an application pause through the current biennium; check it before proposing a new enterprise group.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Enterprise Employee Resource Groups (ERGs) Guidelines
sources.note: Supports open membership including allies, leadership roles and the rule that ERGs may not be used for bargaining, grievances or labor disputes.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Enterprise ERG Bylaws (revised 2023)
sources.note: Published bylaws labeled Revised May 2023: leadership roles and approvals, meeting records, qualifying work time, workload/overtime discretion and unpaid-activity rules. Confirm subsequent updates with MMB.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Join an ERG
sources.note: Participation approval and coverage guidance, Human Resources escalation, and outside-hours exceptions for non-exempt employees assigned to attend or attending in direct relation to normal job duties.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Retention (Executive Order 19-15 resources)
sources.note: Supports the suggestion that leadership meet regularly with an ERG for employees with disabilities to inform workplace decisions. Page contents confirmed by direct retrieval.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 13.03 — Access to Government Data
sources.note: Supports the presumption that government data are public unless classified otherwise. Classification of specific data should be confirmed with the agency data practices contact.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 — Government-to-government relationship with Tribal governments
sources.note: Supports the statement that DHS is among agencies required to have a Tribal consultation policy and a Tribal liaison and to consult on matters with Tribal implications.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations to Human Resources or the agency affirmative action officer.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation
sources.note: Describes employee reporting, supervisory protection and prompt referral responsibilities, and designated Equal Opportunity and Access functions.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 13.05 — Duties of Responsible Authority
sources.note: Limits on collection, storage, use and disclosure of data about individuals. Applies alongside classification and records-retention requirements.
